items.text: A Michigan homeowner's auto policy contains a clear, unambiguous one-year contractual limitation on filing suit. The insured argues a court should void it as unfair given how long the claim took. What does Rory v Continental Ins Co require?

A. The clause must be enforced as written because it is unambiguous and does not violate law or public policy — Rory, 473 Mich 457 (2005), holds unambiguous contracts are enforced as written unless they violate law or public policy, and rejects judicial "reasonableness" as grounds to refuse enforcement.

An insured argues that even though the policy's exclusion is written clearly, a 'reasonable policyholder' in Michigan would have expected broader coverage. What is the state of that doctrine in Michigan?

B. It has no application in Michigan under Wilkie v Auto-Owners Ins Co, 469 Mich 41 (2003) — Wilkie expressly held the rule of reasonable expectations has no application in Michigan and overruled the cases that had recognized it.

A homeowner's declarations page and an endorsement define a key term two conflicting ways. Under Klapp v United Ins Group Agency, Inc, what is the FIRST step a court takes once it finds this ambiguity?

C. Consider relevant extrinsic evidence of the parties' actual intent — Klapp, 468 Mich 459 (2003), requires courts to consider extrinsic evidence and other conventional interpretive tools before resorting to contra proferentem, which is a last-resort tie-breaker.
What is the correct official reporter citation for Klapp v United Insurance Group Agency, Inc, decided by the Michigan Supreme Court in 2003?
D. 468 Mich 459 — The confirmed citation, opened this run against the official reporter, is 468 Mich 459; 663 NW2d 447 (2003). 468 Mich 416 is a frequently repeated wrong page number.

A Wayne County homeowner files a wind-damage claim. The carrier denies, citing a wear-and-tear exclusion, but has not yet shown facts supporting that exclusion. Once the insured has shown the loss fits the coverage grant, who must prove the exclusion applies under Michigan law?

A. The insurer must prove the exclusion applies — Heniser, 449 Mich 155 (1995), gives the two-step order and the insured's burden to show the claim falls within the policy. Hunt v Drielick, 496 Mich 366 (2014), quoting Fresard, 414 Mich 686, 694 (1982), puts the burden of proving an absence of coverage on the insurer. Heniser alone does not state the insurer's half.
An insurer proves a mold exclusion applies, but the exclusion contains an ensuing-loss exception. Which Michigan authority squarely says who must prove the exception?

B. None. No controlling Michigan appellate holding allocating that burden was located; treat it as unsettled and do not attach a Michigan case name to it — Heniser allocates only the insured's coverage burden, and Hunt v Drielick the insurer's exclusion burden. Neither opinion addresses exceptions to exclusions, and no Michigan case squarely allocating that burden was opened. The logical extension, that the party benefiting from the exception proves it, is an inference, not a citable holding.

An adjuster tells a homeowner over the phone, without any written confirmation, that a detached shed not listed on the policy 'will be covered.' Under Kirschner v Process Design Assocs, does this verbal statement alone create coverage that was never written into the policy?

C. Usually no, unless the insured can show the insurer misrepresented the policy's terms or defended without reserving rights — Kirschner, 459 Mich 587 (1999), holds waiver/estoppel usually will not broaden coverage beyond what was written, with narrow exceptions for misrepresentation of terms or defending without a reservation of rights.

A homeowner self-performs a multi-trade rebuild (roof, drywall, flooring, paint) after a covered loss and never hires a general contractor. Under Salesin v State Farm's adopted Gilderman test, is the fact that no GC was hired dispositive against recovering overhead and profit (O&P) in the ACV payment?

D. No, self-performance is 'not dispositive'; the test is whether a GC was reasonably likely to be needed — Salesin, 229 Mich App 346 (1998), held self-performance was 'not dispositive' and adopted the Gilderman 'reasonably likely to incur' standard, while expressly rejecting an automatic-O&P rule.
Which statement most accurately reflects Salesin v State Farm's actual holding on overhead and profit (O&P) in ACV payments?

A. There is no basis in that policy or record to deduct O&P, and self-performance is not dispositive, but the court rejected an always-automatic rule — Salesin's holding is narrow: no basis existed in that policy/record to deduct O&P, and the court expressly said Gilderman does not support an automatic, always-included O&P rule.

A dealership's water loss came from heavy rain (surface water, excluded) combined with a wood-blocked drain (potentially a separate, non-excluded cause). The exclusion stated it applied 'regardless of any other cause or event that contributes concurrently or in any sequence.' What did Sunshine Motors, Inc v New Hampshire Ins Co hold?

B. The policy expressly excluded coverage regardless of whether the blocked drain was a direct, indirect, principal, or contributing cause — Sunshine Motors, 209 Mich App 58 (1995), enforced the ACC clause as written, holding the exclusion applied regardless of the blocked drain's role in the causal chain.
Has the Michigan Supreme Court adopted the concurrent causation (dual causation) theory to override an unambiguous policy exclusion, the way Florida did in Sebo?

C. No. In Vanguard Ins Co v Clarke, 438 Mich 463 (1991), the Court declined to adopt it and reversed a Court of Appeals panel that had — Vanguard reversed the Court of Appeals, saying it did not "discern a compelling legal or policy basis as to why that doctrine should nullify an unambiguous insurance policy exclusion for auto-related injuries in a homeowner's policy." Sunshine Motors is a Court of Appeals case enforcing an anti-concurrent-causation clause, which is narrower and carrier-favorable.

A basement floods from a combination of sump-pump failure (potentially covered) and surface water (excluded, with 'regardless of any other cause' language IN that specific exclusion). Under Sunshine Motors, what is the insured's strongest remaining argument?

D. Segregate and claim only the damage caused solely by the sump failure as a separately payable amount — Sunshine Motors enforces the anti-concurrent-causation clause as written, so options 0, 1 and 2 all ask a Michigan court to do something Sunshine Motors, Rory and Vanguard refuse to do. Confining the claim to damage the excluded peril did not cause is the only argument left that does not require overriding the clause. Sunshine Motors does not itself hold such damage is payable; that turns on the exclusion's own wording.

A Lansing restaurant's business-income policy requires 'direct physical loss of or damage to property' as a coverage trigger. The restaurant closed only because of a Governor's COVID-19 executive order, with no physical damage to the building. Under Gavrilides Management Co v Michigan Ins Co, is the trigger met?

A. No, because the word "physical" requires the loss to have some tangible and measurable presence or effect on the premises — Gavrilides held the word "physical" requires "some manner of tangible and measurable presence or effect in, on, or to the premises," and the restaurants were "closed by impersonal operation of a general law, not because anything about or inside the particular premises at issue had physically changed."
In Gavrilides, did the Michigan Court of Appeals also rule on the insurer's virus exclusion?

A. Yes. Although it said an exclusion matters only if the loss is covered, it addressed the exclusion because the plaintiffs sought to amend, and held the insurer properly denied the claim under it — The opinion notes an exclusion is relevant only if the loss is covered, then says it was "necessary for us to address this alternative basis for denying coverage" because plaintiffs proposed to amend, and concludes "defendant properly denied plaintiffs' claim pursuant to the virus exclusion," rejecting the vagueness and public-policy attacks.
A Michigan fire insurance policy attempts to pay a total-loss claim at less than the property's actual cash value at the time of loss, citing a policy clause. What does MCL 500.2833(1)(a) require?

C. The policy must provide, at a minimum, coverage for the actual cash value of the property at the time of the loss — MCL 500.2833(1)(a) sets a statutory floor requiring, at minimum, ACV coverage at the time of loss, subject to the policy's other provisions.
Under DIFS Bulletin 2024-26-INS, which four items are defined as 'nontangible items' that require a standalone endorsement to depreciate on a qualifying personal-lines HO/DP policy?
D. Labor, taxes, fees, and overhead and profit — Bulletin 2024-26-INS defines nontangible items as labor, taxes, fees, and overhead and profit.

A carrier plans to depreciate O&P on a personal-lines homeowners policy renewing October 1, 2025 by adding a definition inside the policy form itself (no separate endorsement, no premium reduction). Is this compliant with Bulletin 2024-26-INS?

A. No, it must be a standalone, optional endorsement offered with a commensurate premium reduction, not a definition in the form — For policies issued or renewed on or after July 1, 2025, the bulletin requires a standalone, optional, premium-reduced endorsement, not a definition embedded in the policy form, and does not ban the practice outright.
Is DIFS Bulletin 2024-26-INS a statute?

B. No, it is DIFS regulatory/interpretive guidance issued under its authority over policy forms, citing MCL 500.2236(5) — The bulletin is interpretive guidance from DIFS's Director, not a legislative act; it supersedes a prior bulletin (2024-18-INS) through the same administrative process and cites MCL 500.2236(5) as its statutory hook.

Rory says a Michigan court may not refuse to enforce an unambiguous policy provision because it thinks the provision unreasonable. Under the statute Rory points to, who does review Michigan policy forms for reasonableness?

C. The state insurance regulator, on form filing and approval under MCL 500.2236 — Rory holds judicial "reasonableness" is an invalid basis to refuse enforcement, and points to MCL 500.2236, under which basic policy forms are filed with and approved by the Commissioner (now the DIFS Director), who may consider the reasonableness of the policy's conditions and exceptions. DIFS cites the same section in Bulletin 2024-26-INS.

A carrier argues that because a policy term is 'debatable,' it should automatically win under a 'most reasonable interpretation' standard, skipping any ambiguity analysis. Which two Michigan cases together defeat that shortcut?

D. Rory and Klapp: unambiguous language is enforced as written with no reasonableness override, and genuine ambiguity requires extrinsic evidence before contra proferentem, not a bare 'most reasonable reading' — Rory forecloses a judicial reasonableness override of unambiguous language, and Klapp requires extrinsic evidence to be considered before any contra proferentem or 'most reasonable reading' shortcut is used on a genuinely ambiguous term.
